metadata.title: Robin Morgan, poet and feminist whose allies included Jane Fonda and Gloria Steinem, dies at 85

sources.news_title: The feminist leader and author co-founded the Women’s Media Center and hosted its podcast, which recently marked 500 episodes, officials said.

Morgan died Saturday in New York, her son said, after dealing with Parkinson's disease for years, per the AP. Her death followed by days that of longtime ally Gloria Steinem, with whom she and Jane Fonda founded the Women's Media Center. In a statement, per Deadline, Fonda said: "Robin Morgan was an artist, a poet, an activist, and in my eyes, a living legend—a woman whose anthology series, Sisterhood is Powerful, Sisterhood is Global, and Sisterhood is Forever provided the evidence needed to launch a feminist revolution, and it was part of my feminist education that led to the movie, 9 to 5."

Robin Morgan, poet and second-wave feminist icon, dies at 85
Robin Morgan, poet, editor and second-wave feminist leader, has died at 85. Her life linked literature, media and protest in ways that shaped modern feminism.
Robin Morgan, the former child star who went on to become a poet, editor and a leading voice of second-wave feminism in the United States, has died at 85. Morgan died on Saturday in New York after a series of health problems in recent weeks, her son Blake Morgan said.
Her death came days after that of her close friend and fellow activist Gloria Steinem. Morgan was a central figure in the women’s movement of the 1960s and 1970s, while also building a body of work as a poet and writer. Her son said she was still working on new books and poems.
During those years, Morgan was involved in some of the defining moments of second-wave feminism, which built on the gains made by the suffragists decades earlier. In 1968, she was among the organisers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, where activists threw bras into a “Freedom Trash Can”, an act later turned into the myth of bra-burning. In 1970, she edited “Sisterhood is Powerful”, an essay collection seen as one of the key books of the modern women’s movement.
Even so, Blake Morgan said his mother saw herself first as a poet and artist, and that her writing shaped her activism. “She was someone who was able to take very big ideas and distill them succinctly, like a poet, into a few words,” he said, pointing to one of her lines: “hate generalizes, love specifies.”
Morgan was widely credited with coining the term “herstory”, a feminist reworking of “history”, and with popularising the clenched-fist female symbol of the liberation movement. Her poem “Monster”, with the line “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it,” was quoted at rallies and elsewhere. Another poem, “Arraignment”, reflected the movement’s embrace of Sylvia Plath and its anger towards Plath’s husband Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s 1963 suicide. Morgan’s couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” later inspired the title of Sonic Youth’s “J’Accuse Ted Hughes.”
She also took on power across the political spectrum. A government report once called her an “anarchist housewife”. In 1970, she and other protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of Grove Press, whose owner Barney Rosset was fighting efforts by employees to unionise. In her widely reprinted 1970 essay “Goodbye to All That”, she criticised figures ranging from Hugh Hefner to activist Abbie Hoffman, whom she likened to “any other up-and-coming movie star who ditches the first wife and kids.”
In her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had her son, a musician, producer and record company founder. She once described the marriage as a “two member commune”. She later wrote that she was so resistant to labels that she was “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and criticised by conservatives who assumed that she was one. In her 2001 memoir “Saturday’s Child”, she wrote of her surprise at how her life had unfolded and how she had kept “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor.” She added: “Put that in your apple pie and smoke it.”
Morgan wrote more than 20 books, including “Saturday’s Child”, “The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches”, and the poetry collections “Monster” and “Dark Matter”. She followed “Sisterhood is Powerful” with “Sisterhood is Global” in 1984 and “Sisterhood is Forever” in 2002, with contributors including Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. She also served for several years as editor-in-chief of Ms. Magazine.
Steinem described her as an ideal “utility player”, gifted in nearly every way a protest movement might need. Morgan helped found feminist groups including New York Radical Women and Women’s International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell, or W.I.T.C.H. She was also part of the left-wing Youth International Party, or Yippies, led by Hoffman and Jerry Rubin, but later left after becoming disillusioned with how women were treated in the group.
In 1984, she helped found the Sisterhood Is Global Institute, an early feminist think tank. In 2005, she joined Steinem and Jane Fonda in launching the Women’s Media Center, which works to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media.” In later years, she hosted a syndicated radio show and stayed active after being diagnosed with Parkinson’s disease 16 years ago, a condition that also inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.
Long before that public life, Morgan had become a child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she grew up without seeing her father and was falsely told by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also reduced her age by a year, saying she had been born in 1942 so that her early career would seem even more remarkable.
By the age of 3, she was modelling. At 5, she hosted the “Little Robin Morgan” radio show and was also featured on “Juvenile Jury”, first on radio and later on television. From 1949 to 1957, she appeared in the hit TV comedy series “Mama” and also acted in “Robert Montgomery Presents”, “Kraft Theater” and other programmes. She met major stars of the time, including Abbott and Costello and Sal Mineo, and was successful enough to inspire Robin Morgan dolls and other tie-ins. Magazines called her “unspoiled”, “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door”, and described her as free from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society.”
But Morgan later wrote that she was very different from that public image. She said her first “serious” childhood poem began: “Go, rage, winter the world with despair.” On one episode of “Juvenile Jury”, she was meant to joke that a boy who might be spanked should wear padding under his trousers. Instead, she said all physical punishment was wrong. In “Saturday’s Child”, she recalled that producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard she could feel his fingernails, turned her microphone away and finally put his hand over her mouth. “I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” she wrote.
Her overt political life took shape in her late teens. While taking classes at Columbia University and attending poetry workshops, she joined marches for civil rights and against the Vietnam War. She met protesters, artists and poets including W.H. Auden and Anthony Hecht, who once told her: “But, my dear, women should be poems, not write them.” In 1962, she met Pitchford at a Manhattan party. After the others had left, she wrote, he lit candles, put Dvorak’s “New World” symphony on the record player and became her “First”. They then walked for hours and ended up on a downtown park bench, where he told her: “You have such an air of possibility about you, Robin. It makes me believe anything can happen.”
From child star to feminist organiser, editor and poet, Morgan lived a life that moved far beyond the image that first made her famous. Her work in literature, media and the women’s movement remained closely linked through decades of activism and writing.

Robin Morgan, poet and feminist whose allies included Gloria Steinem, dies at 85
Morgan was a wholesome child star who grew up to become an all-American radical.
NEW YORK -- Robin Morgan, a wholesome child star of the 1940s and ‘50s who grew up to become an all-American radical as a poet, essayist, editor and second-wave feminist, has died. She was 85.
Morgan, who was still working on new books and poems, died Saturday in New York after suffering a series of health problems in recent weeks, said her son, Blake Morgan. Her death came just days after that of her close friend and fellow activist Gloria Steinem.
During the 1960s and ’70s, Morgan embodied and inspired historic changes in how women lived and thought. As she was happy to point out, the onetime “Ideal American Girl” and adored “Little Robin Morgan” was a rule breaker and justice seeker with a notable list of achievements, along with a prison record and an FBI file.
Morgan was at the center of the some of the defining moments of what came to be called second-wave feminism, expanding upon the achievements of the suffragists a half-century earlier. In 1968, she was among the organizers of the first protest against the Miss America pageant, joining fellow activists in tossing their bras (soon mythologized as burning) into a “Freedom Trash Can.” The 1970 essay anthology she edited, “Sisterhood is Powerful,” is considered one of the essential texts of the modern women’s movement.
Yet she considered herself primarily a poet and artist, and that work fed into her activism, her son said.
“She was someone who was able to take very big ideas and distill them succinctly, like a poet, into a few words,” said Blake Morgan, pointing to such quotes of hers as “hate generalizes, love specifies.”
Her legacy was one of deeds, words and images. Morgan is widely credited with coining the term “herstory,” the feminist reworking of “history,” and popularizing the clenched fist/female symbol icon of the liberation movement. Her poem “Monster,” with such lines as “I want a women’s revolution like a lover/I lust for it,” was quoted at feminist rallies and beyond. Her poem “Arraignment” helped capture the movement’s embrace of the late Sylvia Plath and condemnation of her husband, poet Ted Hughes, whom Morgan and others blamed for Plath’s suicide in 1963. Morgan’s rhyming couplet “I accuse/Ted Hughes” inspired the title for Sonic Youth’s “J’Accuse Ted Hughes.”
Labeled an “anarchist housewife” in one government report, Morgan confronted the establishment, left and right. In 1970, she and fellow protesters were arrested and jailed after occupying the offices of the avant-garde Grove Press, whose owner, Barney Rosset, was fighting employees’ efforts to unionize. In the widely reprinted 1970 essay “Goodbye to All That,” she called out libertines and activists from Hugh Hefner to Abbie Hoffman, the latter of whom she likened to "any other up-and-coming movie star who ditches the first wife and kids.”
In her personal life, Morgan had male and female lovers and was married for more than 20 years to the gay poet Kenneth Pitchford, with whom she had her son, a musician, producer and record company founder. She once described her marriage as a “two member commune” and was so resistant to labels that she remembered being “straight-baited” by feminists who thought she should be a lesbian and chastised by conservatives who assumed she was a lesbian.
In her 2001 memoir “Saturday’s Child,” she expressed joy and amazement at how her life turned out and how she was able to retain “a threadbare, somewhat surreal sense of humor.”
“Put that in your apple pie and smoke it,” she wrote.
Besides “Saturday’s Child,” she completed more than 20 books, including “The Word of a Woman: Feminists Dispatches,” and the poetry collections “Monster” and “Dark Matter.” She followed “Sisterhood is Powerful” with “Sisterhood is Global” (in 1984), and “Sisterhood is Forever” (2002), featuring such contributors as Steinem, Simone de Beauvoir and Eve Ensler. For several years, she was editor-in-chief of Ms. Magazine.
Steinem would call her an ideal “utility player,” gifted in almost every way a protest movement might require. As an organizer, she helped found such 1960s feminist groups as New York Radical Women and Women's International Terrorist Conspiracy from Hell (W.I.T.C.H.). She was part of the Youth International Party, the left-wing “Yippies” led by Hoffman and Jerry Rubin among others, but soon became disgusted with how the group treated women and left.
In 1984, she was a founder of an early feminist think tank, the Sisterhood Is Global Institute. In 2005, she, Steinem and Jane Fonda launched the Women’s Media Center, which has a mission to support “the visibility, viability and decision-making power of women and girls in media.”
More recently, she hosted a syndicated radio show and remained active despite being diagnosed 16 years ago with Parkinson’s disease, which inspired several poems and a TEDWomen talk in 2015.
In a different era, she might have been just another forgotten child star. Born in 1941 in Lake Worth, Florida, and raised in New York, she never saw her father while growing up and was told — falsely — by her mother that he was dead. Her mother also shaved a year off her age, claiming she was born in 1942, to make her early public career seem even more impressive.
The blonde, talented Robin was modeling by age 3, hosted her own “Little Robin Morgan” radio show at age 5 and around the same time was featured on the radio (later television) game show “Juvenile Jury.” From 1949-57, she appeared in the hit TV domestic comedy series “Mama” and made appearances on “Robert Montgomery Presents,” “Kraft Theater” and other shows.
She would meet some of the era’s biggest stars, from Abbott and Costello to Sal Mineo, and was popular enough to inspire such commercial tie-ins as Robin Morgan dolls. Magazines described her as “unspoiled” and “courteous” and “the ideal girl-next-door,” immune from “violent outbursts of antagonism against established society.”
But off camera, and sometimes on, she was so apart from her image that her first “serious” childhood poem began: “Go, rage, winter the world with despair.” During one broadcast of “Juvenile Jury,” the question was whether a boy deserved to be spanked. Morgan was supposed to joke that he should wear padding under his pants, but she instead declared that all physical punishment was wrong.
As she recalled in “Saturday’s Child,” producer Dan Ehrenreich squeezed her shoulder so hard that Morgan could feel his fingernails. He turned her microphone away and eventually placed his hand over her mouth.
“I realized that I loved and respected that child who fought back in what was the first political act I recall ever daring to make,” Morgan wrote.
Once in her late teens, she began taking classes at Columbia University, attended poetry workshops and became politically active. She marched for civil rights and ending the Vietnam War and met protesters, artists and such poets as W.H. Auden and Anthony Hecht, who gave her a man’s eye view of the creative process, “But, my dear, women should be poems, not write them.”
In 1962, she met Pitchford at a Manhattan party. Once the other guests (“boozy bikers” and “stoned, hallucinating Joffrey dancers”) had left and the host urged her to go with them, Pitchford lit candles, put Dvorak’s “New World” symphony on the record player and became her “First.” They later walked for hours and ended up on a downtown park bench.
“You have such an air of possibility about you, Robin” he told her. “It makes me believe anything can happen.”
___ Associated Press writer Jennifer Peltz contributed.

Robin Morgan, a former editor-in-chief of Ms. Magazine who co-founded the Women’s Media Center with Ms. co-founder Gloria Steinem and Jane Fonda, died today, September 5, just several days after the passing of her friend and colleague Steinem. Morgan was 85.
Her death was announced by her son Blake Morgan and Julie Burton, president and CEO of the Women’s Media Center. A cause of death was not disclosed, but her son noted that she died peacefully in her sleep. Robin Morgan was in her second decade of living with Parkinson’s Disease.
In a statement, Fonda said, “Robin Morgan was an artist, a poet, an activist, and in my eyes, a living legend — a woman whose anthology series, Sisterhood is Powerful, Sisterhood is Global, and Sisterhood is Forever provided the evidence needed to launch a feminist revolution, and it was part of my feminist education that led to the movie, 9 To 5.”
Watch on Deadline
“I have learned so much from Robin over the years,” Fonda added. “I love her and all that she has brought to the world, the women’s movement, and to me on the most personal levels. I already miss her and my heart is broken.”
The editor-in-chief of Ms. Magazine from 1989 to 1994, Morgan, over the last decade, hosted, wrote, and produced the award-winning WMC podcast Women’s Media Center Live with Robin Morgan. The podcast recently produced its 500th episode.
Morgan, Fonda and Steinem co-founded the Women’s Media Center 21 years ago with a mission to give voice to and strengthen democracy for women in media and beyond. “Our job is to make women visible and powerful in the media,” Morgan once told Fox 5 Good Day New York. “And we do that through lots of programs — through training women in media skills, through SheSource, which is the go-to place for experts, through many programs and our radio program [now podcast], Women’s Media Center Live with Robin Morgan.”
Today the Women’s Media Center produces original on-air and online journalism by and about women, and documents and fights structural sexism and racism in media.
“Robin Morgan was one of the architects of the contemporary women’s movement,” Burton said in a statement. “Her global leadership for justice and equality, her work as a pioneering journalist who gave voice and visibility to women, and her fierce artistry as an internationally recognized poet and author of more than 20 books – these all constitute the legacy she has forged over decades of creative, cultural, and political work.”
“We will carry on her work,” Burton said of the WMC.
Fonda recalled another way in which Morgan made an impact.
“In my film career, I know that designers often offer beautiful clothes for interview and award show purposes,” the actor said. “Imagine my surprise and delight a few years ago in learning that the esteemed House of Dior was honoring Robin Morgan, a feminist and women’s liberation leader and one of the organizers of the historic 1969 Miss America pageant protest (and the designer of the feminist symbol of the raised fist within the Venus symbol), with a specially created T-shirt series honoring Robin’s feminist Sisterhood anthology and its global impact.
“The small but mighty activist and literary force was being celebrated by the first woman creative director of Dior women’s haute couture, ready-to-wear, and accessories collections, Maria Grazia Chiuri. What a beautiful and meaningful act showing the power of combining art and activism.”
Morgan’s son Blake survives her; complete survivor information was not immediately available.
